title: Kufic, Naskh, Thuluth
hookLine: angular, round, grand: the main scripts

cards: Say your own name three ways. First as a sergeant would bark it across a parade ground: clipped, square, every edge hard. Then the way a friend says it across the kitchen table: easy, round, clear.
Then the way an announcer calls it into a stadium: long, rising, filling the whole space. Same name, three voices. Arabic calligraphy works like that.
The same holy words can be written in different scripts, and each one speaks in its own voice. Today: Kufic, Naskh and Thuluth.

teach.b: Kufic first. Its name, tradition says, comes from the city of Kufa in Iraq. Kufic is angular: straight strokes, sharp corners, letters stretched long along the line.
It looks carved even in ink, and it carves beautifully, into stone, into wood, into the borders of buildings.

teach.h: SQUARE KUFIC: A MAZE OF BRICKS.
teach.b: Builders even laid it out in bricks and tiles as square Kufic, the letters turned into a maze of right angles, so a wall could spell a name of God over and over.
Kufic is the voice of the inscription: firm, monumental, a little stern.

teach.h: NASKH: ROUND AND CLEAR, FOR READING.
teach.b: Naskh is the friend at the table. Its letters are rounded and even, small clear shapes the eye reads quickly. It became a script for books, for copying the Qur'an to be read.
Naskh wants to be understood. Thuluth is the announcer.
Tall uprights, wide sweeping curves, letters that climb over one another and interlace, often stacked in layers.
It's written large, for the headings of Qur'an chapters and across the walls and domes of mosques, meant to be seen from below and far away. So take one short line: "Say: He is Allah, the One!"
In Kufic it stands like a gate. In Naskh it reads like a letter. In Thuluth it rises like a call.

how: Calligraphers learn the classical scripts one by one under a master, using Naskh for readable texts and Thuluth for large panels and inscriptions, while Kufic and square Kufic appear in carving, tilework and brick.

o: the angular Arabic script, said to be named for Kufa
the round script used for copying books to be read
the tall, sweeping script written across mosque domes

games.q: Kufic, Naskh, Thuluth — tap the pairs.
p: letters as a maze of bricks

s: the three scripts can only be used for different words
the same holy words can be written in any of them, each in its own voice.
square Kufic can be laid out in bricks and tiles
a maze of right angles that spells words across a wall.
Thuluth is the small script for everyday books
Naskh is the clear book script. Thuluth is written large, for headings and walls.

games.q: you're a calligrapher. a mosque wants a line of the Qur'an across its dome, to be read from the floor far below. which script do you choose?
games.why: Thuluth is written large for mosque walls and domes, meant to be seen from below and far away.

practice: Write one short word, your own name if you like, in straight lines only, all corners and no curves, like Kufic. Then write it again, round and easy, like Naskh, and set the two side by side.
Which one sounds louder, which one kinder, and which would you carve over a door?

wordCard.voice: Kufic. The angular script, tradition says named for Kufa, carved in stone and built in bricks. Beside it, Naskh, round, and Thuluth, grand. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: of Kufa, the city tradition links to the angular script.

carryVoice: Your line: each script a voice. Same words, a different way of standing on the page. Until tomorrow.
